items.title: Origin & Constitutional Location
items.body:
## In one line

Fundamental Duties are a short list of moral obligations the Constitution expects every Indian citizen to follow, added 26 years after the Constitution began.

## Why it is asked

The 'which amendment / which committee / inspired by which country' triangle is a reliable one-mark question.

## How Fundamental Duties entered the Constitution

- The **original Constitution (1950) had NO Fundamental Duties** — only rights and directives.
- They were added by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** (enacted during the Emergency) on the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee (1976)**.
- The inspiration came from the **Constitution of the erstwhile USSR**, which balanced citizens' rights with corresponding duties.
- They are placed in **Part IV-A** (a new Part inserted in 1976) under the **single Article 51A**, sitting right after the Directive Principles (Part IV).

## Number of duties over time

| Stage | Amendment | Duties |
|---|---|---|
| Originally added | 42nd (1976) | 10 |
| 11th duty added | 86th (2002) | 11 |

- The **11th duty** obliges a **parent/guardian to provide education opportunities to a child aged 6-14**, added alongside the new **Article 21A (Right to Education)**.

## Terms explained

- **Fundamental Duties** — a short list of moral and civic obligations expected of every citizen.
- **Part IV-A** — the Part added in 1976 that holds the single Article 51A on duties.
- **Swaran Singh Committee (1976)** — the committee whose recommendation led to the duties being added.

## TL;DR

- Fundamental Duties were NOT in the original 1950 Constitution.
- Added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
- Inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
- Located in Part IV-A under the single Article 51A.
- Originally 10 duties; the 11th was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
keyPoints: Fundamental Duties were NOT in the original 1950 Constitution.
Added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
Inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
Located in Part IV-A under the single Article 51A.
Originally 10 duties; the 11th was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
items.mnemonic: '42 gave 10, 86 gave 1' — 42nd Amendment = 10 duties, 86th Amendment = the 11th.

items.title: The 11 Fundamental Duties [Article 51A]
items.body:
## In one line

Article 51A lists the eleven things every citizen should do, from respecting the National Flag to protecting the environment and educating one's child.

## Why it is asked

Clause-matching — 'which duty mentions women / environment / scientific temper' — is a frequent trap.

## Complete list under Article 51A

It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to:

| Clause | Duty (keyword) |
|---|---|
| (a) | Abide by the **Constitution**, respect its ideals, institutions, the **National Flag** and **National Anthem** |
| (b) | Cherish the noble ideals of the **freedom struggle** |
| (c) | Uphold the **sovereignty, unity and integrity** of India |
| (d) | **Defend the country** and render national service when called upon |
| (e) | Promote **harmony & common brotherhood**; renounce practices **derogatory to the dignity of women** |
| (f) | Preserve the rich **composite culture** |
| (g) | Protect the **natural environment** — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife; have compassion for living creatures |
| (h) | Develop **scientific temper**, humanism and the spirit of inquiry & reform |
| (i) | Safeguard **public property** and abjure violence |
| (j) | Strive towards **excellence** in all spheres |
| (k) | *(86th Amdt, 2002)* Provide **education** opportunities to one's child/ward aged **6-14** |

- Clause **(e)** is the only duty expressly mentioning the **dignity of women**.
- Clause **(k)** is the **only duty added after 1976**.

## Terms explained

- **Article 51A** — the single article that lists all the Fundamental Duties.
- **Scientific temper** — the habit of forming views from reason and evidence rather than superstition (clause h).
- **Composite culture** — India’s shared, mixed cultural heritage that citizens should preserve (clause f).

## TL;DR

- 51A(a): respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
- 51A(e) is the only duty referring to the dignity of women.
- 51A(g): protect environment — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife.
- 51A(h): develop scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry.
- 51A(k), the 11th duty (86th Amendment), covers educating a child aged 6-14.
keyPoints: 51A(a): respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
51A(e) is the only duty referring to the dignity of women.
51A(g): protect environment — forests, lakes, rivers, wildlife.
51A(h): develop scientific temper, humanism and spirit of inquiry.
51A(k), the 11th duty (86th Amendment), covers educating a child aged 6-14.
items.mnemonic: For (h) think 'S-H-I' = Scientific temper, Humanism, Inquiry.

items.title: Nature, Enforceability & Verma Committee
items.body:
## In one line

Fundamental Duties are advice, not law: no court can punish you for ignoring them, though Parliament may pass separate penalty laws.

## Why it is asked

The 'justiciable against non-justiciable' contrast with Fundamental Rights is a classic distractor.

## Non-justiciable character

- Fundamental Duties are **non-justiciable** — **not enforceable by any court**, and no legal sanction exists for their violation.
- They are **moral and civic obligations**, meant to be followed **voluntarily**, similar to the non-justiciable **Directive Principles**.
- They apply **only to citizens**, not to foreigners or the State.
- However, **Parliament may prescribe penalties** by law (for example, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act), and courts use the duties as an **aid to interpret laws** and judge their constitutional reasonableness.

## Verma Committee (1999)

- The **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)** was set up to identify measures for the **effective operationalisation** of the duties, since the Swaran Singh Committee had introduced them **without any enforcement mechanism**.
- It emphasised **awareness, education and internalisation** of duties rather than coercion.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Fundamental Rights | Fundamental Duties |
|---|---|---|
| Enforceable in court? | Yes | No (non-justiciable, like the DPSP) |
| Who is bound | The State | Every citizen |
| Location | Part III, Articles 12-35 | Part IV-A, Article 51A |

## Terms explained

- **Non-justiciable** — not enforceable by any court; no legal punishment for ignoring a duty.
- **Moral / civic obligation** — a responsibility meant to be followed voluntarily, like good citizenship.
- **Verma Committee (1999)** — the committee set up to suggest how to make the duties work in practice.

## TL;DR

- Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable — no court can enforce them.
- They are moral obligations, applicable only to citizens.
- Parliament can enact laws prescribing penalties for their breach.
- The Verma Committee (1999) reviewed how to operationalise the duties.
- Duties share their non-justiciable character with the Directive Principles (Part IV).
keyPoints: Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable — no court can enforce them.
They are moral obligations, applicable only to citizens.
Parliament can enact laws prescribing penalties for their breach.
The Verma Committee (1999) reviewed how to operationalise the duties.
Duties share their non-justiciable character with the Directive Principles (Part IV).

items.title: Significance, Criticism & Judicial Note
items.body:
## In one line

Fundamental Duties matter morally and help courts interpret laws, but critics say they have no teeth and are vaguely worded.

## Why it is asked

Mains and the interview use the 'are the duties effective / how to make them effective' angle.

## Significance

- **Balance rights with responsibilities** — a reminder that enjoyment of rights (Part III) carries corresponding duties.
- Promote **civic responsibility, patriotism and national integration**.
- Encourage **environmental conservation** [51A(g)] and **cultural preservation** [51A(f)].
- Serve as a **warning against anti-national and anti-social conduct**.

## Criticism

- **Non-enforceable / limited practical impact** — no legal teeth.
- **Lack of public awareness** reduces effectiveness.
- Some duties are **vaguely worded** (for example, 'noble ideals', 'scientific temper').
- Critics feel they are a **moral appeal** with overemphasis still on rights.

## Judicial relevance

- In **Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2016)**, invoking **51A(a)**, the Supreme Court ordered the **National Anthem** to be played in cinemas with audiences standing; the order was **modified/relaxed in 2018**.
- Courts have read **51A(g)** into environmental jurisprudence and **Article 21**.

## Terms explained

- **Justiciable / non-justiciable** — enforceable in court versus not enforceable; duties are non-justiciable.
- **Aid to interpretation** — courts use the duties to help read and test the reasonableness of laws.
- **Vague wording** — critics say phrases such as ‘noble ideals’ are too loose to apply precisely.

## TL;DR

- Significance: balance rights with duties; foster civic sense, patriotism, national integration.
- 51A(g) and 51A(f) promote environmental and cultural preservation.
- Criticism: non-enforceable, low awareness, vague wording, overemphasis on rights.
- Shyam Narayan Chouksey case (2016) linked the National Anthem to duty 51A(a); relaxed in 2018.
- Courts use duties as an aid to interpret statutes and test their reasonableness.

51A(g) and 51A(f) promote environmental and cultural preservation.
Criticism: non-enforceable, low awareness, vague wording, overemphasis on rights.
Shyam Narayan Chouksey case (2016) linked the National Anthem to duty 51A(a); relaxed in 2018.
Courts use duties as an aid to interpret statutes and test their reasonableness.

items.title: For Mains — Fundamental Duties
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance; clause M3-1)

Fundamental Duties are a favourite for the **'rights vs responsibilities' and 'make them effective' angle**, usually a 10-marker or part of an ethics/governance answer.

| Dimension | What to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Origin** | 42nd Amendment (1976), Swaran Singh Committee, USSR model; Part IV-A, Art 51A, 11 duties |
| **Significance** | Rights carry responsibilities; civic sense, national integration, environment (51A-g), culture (51A-f) |
| **Ineffectiveness** | Non-justiciable, no sanction, low awareness, vague wording, rights-centric culture |
| **Judicial use** | Aid to interpretation; Chouksey (2016/18) anthem; AIIMS Students Union (2002) — duties as important as rights; 51A(g) read into Art 21 |
| **Reform** | Verma Committee (1999): awareness over coercion; civic education, curriculum, calibrated law |
| **Way forward** | Internalisation, not enforcement; link to ethics of citizenship |

**Data / authorities to quote:** Swaran Singh Committee (1976); Verma Committee (1999, enumerated a list of citizen duties and legal provisions); AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002, duties as important as rights); Shyam Narayan Chouksey (2016, modified 2018); Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; link of 51A(k) to Art 21A and RTE Act 2009.

**AP angle:** 51A(g) connects to AP's coastal/mangrove and Eastern Ghats conservation and disaster-preparedness civic drives; 51A(f) to preserving Kuchipudi, Telugu literary heritage and temple architecture; citizen duty themes anchor AP's good-governance and Swachh initiatives.

**Use in answers:** open with 'rights and duties are two sides of the same coin'; use the Chouksey and AIIMS cases to show judicial salience despite non-justiciability; cite the Verma Committee for the reform list; close that duties work by internalisation, not coercion. A simple FR–DPSP–FD triangle diagram ('legal guarantee – State goal – citizen responsibility') earns structure marks.
keyPoints: Frame as rights-and-responsibilities; origin = 42nd Amendment (1976), Swaran Singh Committee, USSR.
Significance: civic sense, national integration, environment (51A-g), composite culture (51A-f).
Ineffectiveness: non-justiciable, no sanction, low awareness, vague wording.
Judicial salience: Chouksey (2016/18) anthem, AIIMS Students Union (2002), 51A(g) read into Art 21.
Reform: Verma Committee (1999) — awareness/education over coercion; calibrated legislation.
AP angle: 51A(g) coastal/Eastern Ghats conservation; 51A(f) Kuchipudi/Telugu heritage.
items.source: M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity (Fundamental Duties); Verma Committee (1999); AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2002)
